content.title: Celebrity Deaths 2026: Stars Who Died Recently
content.text: Skip to main contentKey PointsSeveral celebrities died in 2026.In January, the world said goodbye to rock legend Bob Weir and Catherine O'Hara.February saw the shocking loss of James Van Der Beek and others. The world said goodbye to a slew of beloved entertainers and political icons in 2026, even before the first month of the year was over. Music legend Bob Weir of the Grateful Dead passed away in early January, and the month ended with the shocking death of beloved comedic actress Catherine O’Hara, who died on Jan. 30. Other stars, including athletes, reality personalities and classic rockers, each took their final bows this year. Even for stars who passed away in their 90s, it always somehow still feels far too soon. February brought more devastating and shocking losses, including Rev. Jesse Jackson and actor James Van Der Beek, among others. March saw the death of Chuck Norris, which, even though he was quite old, was still unexpected, because, well, he’s Chuck Norris. Look back at the celebrities we’ve lost in 2026 and tip your hat to their art and creativity, which will live on long after they’ve left Earth. 🤩 📺 SIGN UP for Parade‘s Daily newsletter & get the scoop on the latest TV news & celebrity interviews delivered right to your inbox 🤩🎥 Valerie PerrinePhoto by Anne Cusack on Getty Images Valerie Perrine Sept. 3, 1943 — March 23, 2026 Valerie Perrine died on March 23, 2026, at her home. She was 82. Perrine’s family said in a GoFundMe for the actress’ funeral expenses that she battled Parkinson’s disease in her final years. Perrine’s big screen breakout came with the 1972 film adaption of Slaughterhouse-Five. Two years later, she delivered a performance as Honey Bruce, wife of comedian Lenny Bruce, in the biopic Lenny, earning a Golden Globe and Oscar nomination. Her best known role came in the Christopher Reeve-led Superman films, in which she starred as Lex Luthor’s secretary and sidekick Charlotta Bell. Ronnie BowmanPhoto by Stephen A. Ide on Getty Images Ronnie Bowman July 9, 1961 — March 22, 2026 Musician and songwriter Ronnie Bowman died on March 22, 2026, from injuries in a motorcycle crash. Bowman recorded solo music and was a member of several bands throughout his nearly four-decade career, including the Lost and Found and the Lonesome River Band. He penned songs for artists including Chris Stapleton, Lee Ann Womack and Brooks & Dunn. Nicholas BrendonPhoto by Gilbert Carrasquillo on Getty Images Nicholas Brendon April 12, 1971 — March 20, 2026 Nicholas Brendon, best known for his role as wisecracking Xander Harris in Buffy the Vampire Slayer, died from what his family said were natural causes on March 20, 2026. He was 54. “Most people know Nicky for his work as an actor and for the characters he brought to life over the years,” Brendon’s family said in a statement. “In recent years Nicky has found his passion in painting and art. Nicky loved to share his enthusiastic talent with his family, friends and fans. He was passionate, sensitive and endlessly driven to create.” They then alluded to Brendon’s battle with addiction, some of which was covered in an episode of Dr. Phil in September 2015. “Those who truly knew him understood that his art was one of the purest reflections of who he was,” the statement continued. “While it’s no secret that Nicholas had struggles in the past, he was on medications and treatment to manage his diagnosis and he was optimistic about the future at the time of his passing. Our family asks for privacy during this time as we grieve his loss and celebrate the life of a man who lived with intensity, imagination and heart. Thank you to everyone who has shown love and support.” Related: The Buffy Moments Nicholas Brendon Loved Most Chuck NorrisPhoto by Jon Kopaloff on Getty Images Chuck Norris March 9, 1940 — March 19, 2026 Action hero Chuck Norris died on March 19, 2026. He was 86. Norris, born Carlos Ray Norris, first began martial arts training in Tang Soo Do (tangsudo) when he was in the Air Force. After his honorable discharge in 1962, he launched his own martial arts studio and began competing in tournaments like the International Karate Championships, winning first place in 1967. Norris continued competing while running his own martial arts studio chain. He befriended Bruce Lee on the tournament circuit and later co-starred with Lee in Way of the Dragon (Return of the Dragon) in 1972, which made him a celebrity among martial arts film fans. He continued working and studying both acting and martial arts and had his first lead role in Breaker! Breaker! in 1977. In 1983, Lone Wolf McQuade made Norris a mainstream star and inspired Walker, Texas Ranger, which made him a household name. It premiered in 1993 and ran for eight seasons (plus a TV movie, but who’s counting?). Aside from Walker and the Total Gym infomercials, Norris’ biggest claim to fame may be “Chuck Norris facts.” First emerging online circa 2005, Chuck Norris facts exaggerated his abilities to godlike levels (though many of those jokes were actually stolen from comedian Judah Friedlander, which he wrote for his stage persona The World Champion). Outside of the Internet, most of Norris’ fan base consisted of martial arts enthusiasts and political conservatives, as he spoke in favor of teaching the Bible in schools, endorsed the National Rifle Association and Glock firearms, opposed same-sex marriage, was close pals with Benjamin Netanyahu (for whom there is an International Criminal Court warrant for crimes against humanity) and endorsed Mike Huckabee and Donald Trump. In 2010, Norris became a columnist for Creators Syndicate, and in 2012 starred in The Expendables 2. His most recent screen appearances were 2019’s Chuck Norris’ Epic Guide to Military Vehicles on the History Channel and the 2020 series finale of Hawaii Five-O. Related: Chuck Norris’ Net Worth at the Time of His Death Kiki Shepard attends the opening night performance of “Blues for an Alabama Sky” at the Mark Taper Forum on April 13, 2022, in Los Angeles, California.Paul Archuleta / Contributor, Getty Images Kiki Shepard July 15, 1951 — March 16, 2026 Kiki Shepard, best known as the longtime host of the popular variety show Showtime at the Apollo from 1987 to 2002, died of a heart attack on March 16, 2026. She was 74. Born Chiquita Renee Shepard in 1951, she began her dancing and acting career in the early ‘70s, appearing in the Broadway productions Bubbling Brown Sugar, Comin’ Uptown, Reggae, Your Arms Too Short to Box With God and Porgy and Bess. She also danced in the 1978 film The Wiz. An advocate for those affected by sickle cell disease, Shepard founded the KIS Foundation in 2006 to help raise awareness for the condition. She is survived by a sister, a nephew and two nieces. Matt ClarkPhoto by Frazer Harrison on Getty Images Matt Clark Nov. 25, 1936 — March 15, 2026 Matt Clark died on March 15, 2026, from complications following back surgery. He was 89. Clark is best known for his scene in Back to the Future Part III in which he plays a bartender witnessing Marty McFly beefing with cowboys. Clark’s other credits include the sitcom Grace Under Fire, Little House on the Prairie and literally dozens more movies and TV shows. Tommy DeCarlo of BostonPhoto by Daniel Knighton/Getty Images Tommy DeCarlo April 23, 1965 — March 9, 2026 Tommy DeCarlo, the lead singer of rock group Boston since 2007, died of brain cancer at age 60 on March 9, 2026. DeCarlo took over for the band’s original lead vocalist, Brad Delp, after Delp died by suicide on March 9, 2007. He was featured on Boston’s last album, Life, Love & Hope, in 2013, along with posthumous vocals by Delp. DeCarlo is survived by his wife, Annie, and two children. “After being diagnosed with brain cancer last September, he fought with incredible strength and courage right up until the very end,” they shared. “During this difficult time, we kindly ask that friends and fans respect our family’s privacy as we grieve and support one another.” Joseph “Country Joe” McDonaldPhoto by United Archives on Getty Images Joseph ‘Country Joe’ McDonald Jan. 1, 1942 — March 7, 2026 Joseph “Country Joe” McDonald died on March 7, 2026, from Parkinson’s disease. He was 86. The folk singer performed at Woodstock and was part of the 1960s counterculture, with lyrics reflecting the civil rights movement, opposition to the Vietnam War and supporting free speech and protests. McDonald was prolific artist both as a solo artist and part of his band, Country Joe & the Fish, recording more than 30 albums and writing or co-writing hundreds of songs throughout his life. Related: 1990 Tearjerker Voted ‘Best Country Song’ of All Time Troy MurrayPhoto by Bruce Kluckhohn on Getty Images Troy Murray July 31, 1962 — March 7, 2026 Troy Murray, former Chicago Blackhawks player and analyst, died from cancer on March 7, 2026. He was 63. Blackhawks CEO and Chairman Danny Wirtz paid tribute to the Stanley Cup winner, writing on X, “He never missed a chance to say ‘hello’ in our press box and always knew the perfect time for a joke just when someone around the office needed it most. And he absolutely loved bringing Blackhawks hockey to you, our fans, night after night with a dedication to his craft that never wavered to the very end.” Jennifer RunyonPhoto by Bobby Bank on Getty Images Jennifer Runyon Jennifer Runyon, best known for Ghostbusters, Charles in Charge and A Very Brady Christmas, died on March 6, 2026. She was 65. Runyon said in 2014 that she retired from acting to pursue a teaching career. Her family said in a statement in part, “It was a long and arduous journey that ended with her surrounded by her family. She will always be remembered for her love of life and her devotion to her family and friends. Rest in peace our Jenn.” Chase PistonePhoto by Dilip Vishwanat on Getty Images Chase Pistone Aug. 20, 1983 — March 2, 2026 Former NASCAR driver Chase Pistone died on March 2, 2026, at just 42 years old. His family did not publicly announce his cause of death, but urged reports to include information about the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline: You can call or text 988 any time, day or night, 24/7/365 if you or someone you love is struggling. John HammondPhoto by Michael Ochs Archives on Getty Images John Hammond Nov. 13, 1942 — Feb. 28, 2026 Blues singer John Hammond died March 1, 2026, from cardiac arrest. He was 83. Hammond, son of was record producer John Henry Hammond Jr., began playing guitar in high school and basically never stopped. Throughout his six-decade career, Hammond collaborated with artists including Jimi Hendrix, Duane Allman, John Lee Hooker and Eric Clapton. He won a Grammy in 1985 and was nominated for six others, and was inducted to the Blues Hall of Fame in 2010. Neil SedakaPhoto by Sarah Stier on Getty Images Neil Sedaka March 13, 1939 — Feb. 27, 2026 Singer and songwriter Neil Sedaka died on Feb. 27, 2026. He was 86, just two weeks shy of his 87th birthday. “Our family is devastated by the sudden passing of our beloved husband, father and grandfather, Neil Sedaka,” his family said in a statement. “A true rock and roll legend, an inspiration to millions, but most importantly, at least to those of us who were lucky enough to know him, an incredible human being who will be deeply missed.” Sedaka had reportedly been hospitalized earlier that day for a sudden medical emergency. Sedaka was a founding member of The Tokens in the 1950s and went on to become a solo star, penning and recording hits including “Breaking Up Is Hard to Do,” “Calendar Girl” and “Bad Blood.” He is in the Songwriters Hall of Fame and was nominated for five Grammys throughout his long and illustrious career. Carrie Anne FlemingPhoto by Andrew Chin on Getty Images Carrie Anne Fleming Aug. 16, 1974 — Feb. 26, 2026 Carrie Anne Fleming, best known for her roles in Supernatural and iZombie, died on Feb. 26, 2026, of complications from breast cancer. She was 51. Fleming acted for more than three decades, with appearances in Happy Gilmore, The L Word, Good Luck Chuck, Supergirl and Smallville among her credits. Related: Neil Sedaka’s Biggest Hit Surprised Fans by Topping the Charts Twice Todd Meadows 2000/2001 — Feb. 25, 2026 Todd Meadows of Deadliest Catch died on Feb. 25, 2026, at age 25. His specific birthdate isn’t publicly known. TMZ reported that Meadows, the newest deckhand of the Aleutian Lady, died while fishing and filming in the Bering Sea. Captain Rick Shelford wrote on Facebook that Meadows’ “smile was contagious, and the sound of his laughter coming up the wheelhouse stairs or over the deck hailer is something we will carry with us always.” “Todd’s love for his children, his family, and his life was evident in everything he did,” Shelford’s post continued. “He worked hard, loved deeply, and brought joy to those around him.” Oliver “Power” GrantPhoto by John Lamparski on Getty Images Oliver “Power Grant” Nov. 24, 1970 — Feb. 24, 2026 Oliver “Power” Grant died on Feb. 24, 2026 at age 55 after a battle with pancreatic cancer. Grant’s family and the rest of the Wu-Tang Clan said in a statement to Rolling Stone, “A true fighter until the end, he was surrounded by his mother, his children, his family, and his closest friends.” Loved ones remembered Grant, who was born and raised in the Park Hill neighborhood of New York City’s Staten Island borough, as “a visionary force, a pillar of the Wu-Tang family, and a global architect of culture.” “It was the honor of his life to pour his love, wisdom, and brilliance into his family and his community,” the statement continued. “His impact was singular; there will never be another to take his place. Power will always be loved, and his legacy will forever remain.” Bobby J. Brown and his wifeCourtesy of Instagram Bobby J. Brown 1963 — Feb. 24, 2026 The Wire star Bobby J. Brown died on Feb. 24, 2026. He was 62, (his exact birthdate hasn’t been publicly disclosed). According to a fire marshal’s report, Brown was jump-starting a vehicle in the barn of his Chaptico, Md., home when a fire sparked in the building. He called for a fire extinguisher, but by the time it arrived, the fire spread throughout the structure. Brown’s wife was severely burned trying to save him from the blaze. Brown’s official cause of death was smoke inhalation. Lauren ChapinPhoto by Ron Gallela Ltd. via Getty Images Lauren Chapin May 23, 1945 — Feb. 24, 2026 Lauren Chapin, who starred as Kathy “Kitten” Anderson in Father Knows Best, died on Feb. 24, 2026 at age 80. Her son Matthew announced her passing on social media, writing, “After a long hard fought battle over the past 5 years, the time has come. My mother Lauren Chapin passed away from her battle with cancer tonight.” In addition to starring in Father Knows Best, Chapin also appeared in General Electric Theater, The Amorous Adventures of Don Quixote and Sancho Panza, Scout’s Honor and the 2016 series School Bus Diaries. Robert CarradinePhoto by Steve Granitz on Getty Images Robert Carradine March 24, 1954 — Feb. 23, 2026 Robert Carradine died on Feb. 23, 2026. He was just a month shy of his 72nd birthday. Carradine’s family said in a statement, “It is with profound sadness that we must share that our beloved father, grandfather, uncle, and brother Robert Carradine has passed away. In a world that can feel so dark, Bobby was always a beacon on light to everyone around him.” The statement continued, “We are bereft at the loss of this beautiful soul and want to acknowledge Bobby’s valiant struggle against his nearly two-decade battle with Bipolar Disorder. We hope his journey can shine a light and encourage addressing the stigma that attaches to mental illness. At this time we ask for the privacy to grieve this unfathomable loss. With gratitude for your understanding and compassion.” Carradine was best known for his role as Sam McGuire, Lizzie McGuire’s father, in Lizzie McGuire, and as Lewis Skolnick in the Revenge of the Nerds franchise. He is survived by daughter Ever Carradine, niece Martha Plimpton and adult children Ian and Marika. Related: Was Robert Carradine Related to David Carradine and Keith Carradine? Inside the Famous Acting Family Ronyell WhitakerPhoto by Getty Images on Getty Images Ronyell Whitaker March 19, 1979 — Feb. 22, 2026 Former Minnesota Vikings defensive back Ronyell Whitaker died on Feb. 22, 2026, his family announced. He was 46. He played for the Vikings in 2006, then was traded to the Detroit Lions, after which he played in the Canadian Football League for the Winnipeg Blue Bombers. He retired as a player in 2010, but went on to coach a local Minnesota high school team. Whitaker’s family said in a statement in part, “While many knew him for his athletic accomplishments, those closest to him knew him best for his generous heart, unwavering loyalty and deep love for his family. He was a protector, a mentor and a source of strength and laughter to all who had the blessing of knowing him.” Kara BraxtonPhoto by Jennifer Pottheiser on Getty Images Kara Braxton Feb. 18, 1983 — Feb. 21, 2026 Kara Braxton died on Feb. 21, 2026. The two-time WNBA champion was 43. Braxton played 10 seasons in the league, rocking jerseys for Detroit Shock, Tulsa Shock, Phoenix Mercury and New York Liberty throughout her career. “It is with profound sadness that we mourn the passing of 2x WNBA Champion Kara Braxton,” the WNBA said in a statement. “Our thoughts are with her family, friends, and former teammates at this time.” The Arizona Republic reported that Braxton died in a car accident after her vehicle hit a concrete median, with authorities claiming she drifted out of her lane of traffic. She is survived by her husband, Jarvis Jackson, twin sister and two sons, one of whom is Ohio State University football star Jelani Thurman. Willie ColónPhoto by Gladys Vega on Getty Images Willie Colón April 28, 1950 — Feb. 21, 2026 Willie Colón died on Feb. 21, 2026. He was 75. The salsa legend’s cause of death hasn’t been disclosed. Colón’s family said in a statement, “It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, and renowned musician, Willie Colón. He departed peacefully this morning, surrounded by his loving family. Although we mourn his absence, we also rejoice in the eternal gift of his music and the cherished memories it created, which will live on forever.” The multi-instrumentalist first learned to play the flute in elementary school, then moved the bugle before falling in love with trumpet when he was 13, Rolling Stone reported. Colón’s career began when he was just 16 years old, releasing his debut album with Héctor Lavoe, El Malo in 1967. He recorded more than 40 albums and sold more than 30 million records throughout his nearly six-decade career. Super Bowl superstar Bad Bunny paid tribute to Colón, who he namedrops in his hit “NUEVAYoL.” “This music is very special. It’s the influence of all of us who grew up listening to salsa in the Caribbean. Today, one of the great legends who contributed to this beautiful genre passed away,” Bad Bunny said during his Sao Paulo, Brazil, concert on Feb. 21. “From me and Los Sobrinos, we wish Willie Colón rests in peace. Much strength to his family.” Bill MazeroskiPhoto by Jamie Squire on Getty Images Bill Mazeroski Sept. 5, 1936 — Feb. 21, 2026 Bill Mazeroski, Baseball Hall of Famer, died on Feb. 21, 2026. He was 89. Mazeroski was a legend on the Pittsburgh Pirates, who paid tribute to him after his passing. “It is with a heavy heart that we relay the news of the passing of legendary Pirates and National Baseball Hall of Famer, Bill Mazeroski,” the team said in a statement on X. “Maz was a 7-time All-Star who hit the greatest home run in baseball history. He was a beloved member of the Pirates family and he will be deeply missed.” On Oct. 13, 1960, while facing off with the New York Yankees, Mazeroski made Major League Baseball history: He hit the first-ever—and so far only ever—walk-off homerun to win a World Series. It was the first championship the Pirates won in 33 years. He also set a league record of 1,706 double plays throughout his career, according to NorthPennNow. Rondale MoorePhoto by Cooper Neill on Getty Images Rondale Moore June 9, 2000 — Feb. 21, 2026 Rondale Moore, Minnesota Vikings and former Arizona Cardinals wide receiver, died by suicide in his hometown of New Albany, Ind., on Feb. 21, 2026, the Athletic reported. He was 25 years old. Vikings head coach Kevin O’Connell said in a statement, “I am devastated by the news of Rondale’s death. While Rondale had been a member of the Vikings for a short time, he was someone we came to know well and care about deeply.” “He was a humble, soft-spoken and respectful young man who was proud of his Indiana roots,” O’Connell’s statement continued. “As a player, he was disciplined, dedicated and resilient despite facing adversity multiple times as injuries sidelined him throughout his career. We are all heartbroken by the fact he won’t continue to live out his NFL dream and we won’t all have a chance to watch him flourish. My prayers are with Rondale’s family, friends, teammates and coaches as we all deal with this tragic news.” “Rondale Moore was a complete joy to coach,” Rondale’s college coach Jeff Brohm wrote on X. “The ultimate competitor that wouldn’t back down from any challenge. Rondale has a work ethic that was unmatched by anyone. A great teammate that would come through in any situation. We all loved Rondale, we loved his smile and competitive edge that always wanted to please everyone he came in contact with. We offer all of our thoughts and prayers to Rondale and his family, we love him very much.” If you or someone you love have thoughts of suicide or are struggling with your mental health, please know you are not alone and that you are valued. Please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988 or at 988lifeline.org for help. The world is better because you are in it. Maxi ShieldPhoto by Don Arnold on Getty Images Maxi Shields June 1, 1974 — Feb. 21, 2026 RuPaul’s Drag Race Down Under star Maxi Shield died on Feb. 21, 2026 at 51. Shield, born Kristopher Elliot, revealed six months prior to her death that she had throat cancer, and often chronicled her treatment on social media. World of Wonder, the production company behind Drag Race, said in a statement to Deadline, “We are heartbroken to announce the passing of Kristopher Elliot AKA Maxi Shield. A part of our Down Under legacy, her electrifying presence on and off the stage will inspire us forever, and our deepest condolences go out to her friends and family. RIP, we love you Maxi.” A staple in the Sydney LGBTQIA+ scene, Shield competed in the first season of Drag Race Down Under, coming in sixth place, and starred in the comedy The Winner Takes It All. On Jan, 30, 2026, Shield wrote in what would be her final Instagram post, “Weekly update-ish. We are stronger we think! This is my 29th day since my last treatment. As you know, the first few weeks were tough. It’s probably the worst I’ve felt over this whole experience. But each day I’m feeling a little better..Seeing a tiny light at the end of the tunnel really has lifted my spirits..[T]o anyone out there going through this or even recently being diagnosed, you are stronger than you know, this is just a moment in an incredible life you have left to live… you can do it.” Eric DanePhoto by Axelle/Bauer-Griffin on Getty Images Eric Dane Nov. 9, 1972 — Feb. 19, 2026 Eric Dane died at age 53 on Feb. 19, 2026, after battling amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), also known as Lou Gehrig’s disease, for over a year. It was the 20th anniversary of his debut as “McSteamy” on Grey’s Anatomy. Dane was born Nov. 9, 1972, in San Francisco, and fell into acting by accident. “I was a water polo player in high school and my season was short, and I ended up getting roped into playing Joe Keller in All My Sons. Dead serious,” he told Gulf Times in 2014. “And I fell in love with it. I was, like, ‘This is the greatest feeling ever!’” Dane moved to Los Angeles after graduating high school and was a frequent guest star on TV shows for years, including Married… With Children, The Wonder Years, Saved By the Bell, Roseanne and more. His first regular television role was as Jason Dean, a love interest for Phoebe (Alyssa Milano) on Charmed for two seasons. On Feb. 19, 2006, Dane made his first appearance in his most famous role as Dr. Mark “McSteamy” Sloan on Grey’s. It was supposed to be another guest arc, but fans became so obsessed that his hot plastic surgeon character became a fulltime cast member. He was killed off in 2012, which Dane speculated was because he became “too expensive” for the network, but admitted he was also struggling with addiction at the time. Dane went on to appear in movies including Valentine’s Day, Marley & Me and Burlesque and had two more star turns in TV series The Last Ship and Euphoria. In 2025, Dane revealed his ALS diagnosis. He continued working, including filming Euphoria Season 3 and a guest starring role as a firefighter with ALS in Brilliant Minds, until he was no longer able to do so. Dane is survived by estranged wife Rebecca Gayheart, who he married in 2004, and daughters Billie, born in 2010 and Georgia, born in 2011. Gayheart filed for divorce in 2018, but rescinded her filing after Dane’s ALS diagnosis. Related: Why Eric Dane Barely Watched Grey’s Anatomy Francine BeppuPhoto by Jason Merritt on Getty Images Francine Beppu Feb. 28, 1982 — Feb. 17, 2026 Francine Beppu, star of Showtime’s The Real L Word, died on Feb. 17, 2026, her family announced. She was 43 years old and less than two weeks from turning 44. In a statement (via TMZ), they wrote in part, “It is with a heavy heart that we share the passing of our beloved Francine ‘Naoko’ Beppu. The outpouring of care and concern from her friends and colleagues everywhere is a testament to the tremendous impact she had on everyone around her. We are deeply grateful to know how cherished she was and how brightly she will continue to shine through all who knew her.” Beppu reportedly passed away at her home in Honolulu, Hawaii. No cause of death has been revealed at this time. Rev. Jesse Jackson in June 2022Photo by Unique Nicole on Getty Images Rev. Jesse Jackson Oct. 8, 1941 — Feb. 17, 2026 Iconic civil rights activist Rev. Jesse Jackson died on Feb. 17, 2026. He was 84 years old. His family said in a statement that Jackson passed away peacefully at home. “Our father was a servant leader—not only to our family, but to the oppressed, the voiceless, and the overlooked around the world,” their statement continued. “We shared him with the world, and in return, the world became part of our extended family. His unwavering belief in justice, equality, and love uplifted millions, and we ask you to honor his memory by continuing the fight for the values he lived by.” Jackson marched with Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. and was with him the day he was assassinated. Jackson ran for the Democratic presidential nomination twice (1984 and 1988) and personally secured the release of three American troops from Yugoslavia in 1999. A year later, then-President Bill Clinton awarded Jackson the Presidential Medal of Freedom. In his later years, Jackson was plagued with health issues, most notably progressive supranuclear palsy, a neurodegenerative disorder that’s been likened to a more severe form of Parkinson’s disease. He is survived by his wife Jacqueline, their five adult children and an adult daughter from another relationship. Related: Rev. Al Sharpton Says Rev. Jesse Jackson ‘Taught Me Activism’ Robert Duvall won the Oscar for Best Actor for his performance in the film “Tender Mercies” at the 56th Academy Awards.William Nation/Sygma via Getty Images Robert Duvall Jan. 5, 1931 — Feb. 15, 2026 Robert Duvall, who achieved fame as one of Hollywood’s greatest character actors for his roles in True Grit, the first two Godfather movies, Apocalypse Now, A Civil Action and other films, died at age 95. His wife Luciana Pedraza said in a statement that he “passed away peacefully at home.” No cause was given. Duvall’s acting career spanned 70 years. His first film role was as Boo Radley in 1962’s To Kill a Mockingbird. Over a decade later, he earned his first Academy Award nomination for his performance as Corleone family lawyer Tom Hagen in The Godfather (1972). He was nominated for six more Oscars, winning once in the category of Best Actor for his role in Tender Mercies (1983) as Mac Sledge, a country music star whose life has been ravaged by alcoholism. In 2022, Duvall starred in his final two films, playing Rex Merrick in Hustle and Jean-Pepe in The Pale Blue Eye. His numerous TV credits include roles in Alfred Hitchcock Presents, Route 66, The Twilight Zone and The F.B.I., among others. Following his death, tributes for Duvall poured in from friends, peers and admirers, including Francis Ford Coppola, who called Duvall a “great actor” and an “essential part” of Coppola’s production company American Zoetrope, as well as Al Pacino, who said Duvall’s “phenomenal gift” for acting “will always be remembered.” Tre’ Johnson at training camp for the Washington Redskins (now Commanders) on July 29, 2000Photo by The Washington Post on Getty Images Tre’ Johnson Aug. 30, 1971 — Feb. 15, 2026 Former Washington Commanders (then Redskins) offensive lineman Tre’ Johnson died suddenly on Feb. 15, 2026, during what his wife Irene called a “brief family trip.” He was 52. His wife Irene wrote on Facebook, “His four children, Chloe, EJ, EZ and Eden, extended family, friends and I are devastated and in shock. If you know Tre’ you know what a devoted and loving father, he was to his children. Tre’ lived for his kid’s sports activities and supported them through every practice and game until he took his last breath. He shared his passion for Frenchie’s and riding his motorcycle with me and his fellow biking buddies.” Irene recalled his NFL career, beginning as a second round draft pick from Temple University and playing eight seasons for Washington from 1994 to 2001 (plus the 1999 Pro Bowl) before going to the Cleveland Browns, then retiring. “He loved the game and prided himself on his tremendous knowledge of it,” her statement reads. “After retirement, he also found his second career passion, education. He worked as a History Teacher at the Landon School in Bethesda Maryland, where he was beloved by the young male students he mentored and the faculty. His recent battles with health issues forced him to take a leave of absence. We will miss him so much. “ Tom NoonanPhoto by Jeff Vespa on Getty Images Tom Noonan April 12, 1951 — Feb. 14, 2026 Actor, director and writer Tom Noonan died on Feb. 14, 2026. He was 74 years old. Noonan was an iconic character actor best known for his chilling roles as villains, starring as The Ripper in Last Action Hero (1993), Frankenstein’s Monster in Monster Squad (1987), RoboCain in RoboCop 2 (1990) and as Francis Dollarhyde in Manhunter (1986). “I am sort of weird—but not that bad,” Noonan told Filmmaker magazine in 2015, adding, “The secret to being scary is to be really scared. Because when you’re really scared, people are really scared of you.” Noonan was a playwright and screenwriter, penning What Happened Was…, Wifey and more. His cause of death has not yet been reported. Timothy VeryPhoto by Theo Wargo on Getty Images Tim Very Nov. 21, 1983 — Feb. 14, 2026 Manchester Orchestra announced the death of their drummer Timothy “Tim” Very on Feb. 14, 2026. He was 42 and no cause of death has yet been disclosed. Very joined the band in 2011 and has had several side projects as well, including a YouTube channel. “The entire Manchester Orchestra family has been devastated by the sudden passing of our brother, Timothy Very,” the band wrote on Instagram. “The most beloved human being any of us were lucky enough to know in this life. We’ve all been dreading sharing this news as we are all still in absolute disbelief. Tim was instantly likable and interacted with everyone he met with kindness and warmth. His laugh was infectious and he immediately made people feel invited and encouraged. His humor and energy were the very foundation that held together the entire MO universe. Strangers quickly became friends and friends became family.” The statement continued, “He had an undeniable light that was only matched by his dedication and love for the craft that he was clearly put on earth to do. No words can ever do him justice. Please know, if you are someone who loved Tim, he loved you too.” “The only thing that Tim loved more than creating music was being with his family,” MO concluded. “You’d be pressed to find a more joyful dad. We love you Tim, thank you for loving us. You are a force of positivity that will be a constant presence in the rest of our days.” Bud CortPhoto by David Livingston on Getty Images Bud Cort March 29, 1948 — Feb. 11, 2026 Bud Cort died on Feb. 11, 2026, after a long, unspecified illness. He was 77. Cort was born Walter “Wally” Edward Cox in Rye, N.Y., later adopting his stage name in part as a tribute to the Cort Theatre (now the James Earl Jones Theatre), Entertainment Weekly reported.
